lessons.title: Planning and improving a sample
lessons.summary: Identify data types, choose a sampling method and improve a question after a trial.
lessons.objective: Identify data types, choose a sampling method and improve a question after a trial.
lessons.before: Start with the question you want your data to answer.
lessons.ideas:
Categorical data give a label. Discrete numerical data can only take separate values, such as counts. Continuous data are measurements that can take any value in an interval.

A convenience sample is quick but may miss some groups. Random selection helps avoid preference. A systematic sample takes every kth item after a start and can miss patterns if the list is periodic.

Check that the question is clear, is fair and gives the type of data you need. Change unclear instructions or units, then try again.
lessons.method:
State what each data row is about and use the same units throughout.

Name who may be missing and how that could change the result.

Make a prediction and decide what you would measure before collecting data.
mistakes: Writing metres to the nearest centimetre does not turn height into a count.
A bigger sample can still be biased if all members come from one group.
A question with no time frame can lead to answers about different situations.

examples.title: Decide which type of data to collect
examples.question:
A survey team invites 8 learners and records each learner’s chosen route colour.

  1. What type of data will this variable give?

    [2]

  2. Give a suitable way to record the variable for one learner.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Colours are categories, even when a spreadsheet replaces each colour name with a code.

Categorical

(b) Record the same sort of value and use the same units for each learner.

Record the route colour, for example blue.

examples.title: Choose a fairer sample
examples.question:
A school wants to estimate lunch choices across 37 classes. A team first asks only the 2 learners in a sports club.

  1. Which method would give better coverage of the whole school?

    [2]

  2. Give one benefit of the first sample and explain its limitation.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Include every class in the sampling plan, then draw names without preference within each class.

Select a sample at random from each class, allowing for class sizes

(b) Convenience makes an easy trial. A wider representative sample is needed for a claim about the whole school.

It is quick to collect, but sports club members alone may have different choices from other learners.

examples.title: Improve a trial survey
examples.question:
In a trial with 41 learners, 3 people left the question ‘How long is your trip?’ blank because they were unsure about units.

  1. Which revised instruction gives clearer numerical data?

    [2]

  2. What should you check when you test the revised item with a small group?

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The revised question identifies what to measure, the period and the unit.

Record your travel time to school today, in minutes

(b) The trial should reveal whether the question produces data suitable for the investigation.

Check that people understand the question, use minutes and record the same trip.

lessons.title: Tables, bar charts and pie charts
lessons.summary: Use diagrams and tables to organise counts and choose a display that fits the comparison.
lessons.objective: Use diagrams and tables to organise counts and choose a display that fits the comparison.
lessons.ideas:
In a Venn diagram, the middle overlap shows both properties. In a Carroll diagram, each cell shows one yes-or-no combination. Tally marks can record counts as data arrive.

Add across rows for one property and down columns for the other. An unknown cell is often a total with the known entries removed.

Dual bars make same-category comparisons easy. Compound bars show category totals as stacks, with each component coloured or patterned and labelled in a key.

A sector is the same fraction of 360° as the category is of the total count. Divide frequency by the total, then multiply by 360°.
lessons.method:
Check that all the disjoint parts add to the total.

Check the grand total using the row totals and again using the column totals.

Give a clear scale and a key for both groups.

Check the angles add to one complete turn.
mistakes: A person in the overlap has both properties, but is counted once in a total of people.
Read the row and column names before selecting a value.
The height of one segment is its top value minus its bottom value.
Do not treat a count as an angle unless the totals make that conversion valid.

examples.title: Organise overlapping club choices
examples.question:
Of 46 learners, 13 chose cycling and 10 chose art. Exactly 4 chose both.

  1. How many learners did not choose either club?

    [2]

  2. Complete a Carroll diagram with choices Cycling and Art.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Only cycling is 9. Only art is 6. Add both of these and the 4 in the overlap.

Subtract this total from 46.

\(27\)

(b) A Carroll diagram has a box for each combination of yes and no.

Both 4, cycling only 9, art only 6, neither 27.

    [2]

  2. How many learners in the two groups chose the library?

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The Group Y row has total 16. Subtract the 7 in its music room cell.

\(9\)

(b) Add the two entries in the library column. Do not add the row totals.

examples.title: Compare and combine bar chart categories
examples.question:
The table gives the number of votes from each tutor group.
ChoiceTutor ATutor B
Drama37
Art63

  1. In a compound bar chart, what is the full height of the Drama bar in votes?

    [2]

  2. Which chart arrangement makes it easiest to compare Tutor A and Tutor B for one choice?

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) A compound bar stacks the two sections. Add the two Drama counts.

\(10\)

(b) In a dual bar chart both bars start at the common baseline, which makes their heights easy to compare.

examples.title: Use a pie-chart sector to show a share
examples.question:
Of 30 votes for a project, 18 choose design A. The other votes choose design B.

  1. Find the exact angle of the sector for design A.

    [2]

  2. Why would a whole pie chart for each of two classes not show which class cast more votes?

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Design A has \(\frac{3}{5}\) of the votes. Use the same fraction of the full 360° circle.

\(216\) degrees

(b) Keep the total count with the pie charts if counts will also be compared.

Each circle is the same size and only shows shares of its own total.

lessons.title: Grouped data, time series and scatter graphs
lessons.summary: Interpret grouped measurements, stem-and-leaf diagrams, graphs and infographics.
lessons.objective: Interpret grouped measurements, stem-and-leaf diagrams, graphs and infographics.
lessons.before: Group measurements in adjacent intervals and write clearly which end values are included.
lessons.ideas:
In equal-width frequency diagrams, each interval gets one bar. The height shows the count for that interval. Use boundaries rather than labels that leave gaps.

Write the leaves in order beside their stem. Include a key such as 3 | 7 means 37. The diagram shows individual values and the shape of the data.

Connect observations over time in a time series. To explore a relationship, plot paired values as scatter points and look for a pattern without joining the dots in time order.

Look for a consistent key, fair scale, labels and enough context. A picture that changes width and height can greatly exaggerate change.
lessons.method:
Check an exact boundary belongs to only one group.

Use the key before reading the shortest or longest value.

Label both axes and give both units.

Use the key rather than guessing from the visual size.
mistakes: A frequency for an interval does not give the individual measurements inside it.
A repeated leaf records a repeated value. Keep every one.
An upward pattern can suggest a relationship. It does not show that one variable causes the other.
A bigger-looking symbol alone does not tell you the exact value.

examples.title: Read grouped measurements
examples.question:
A class groups stopwatch readings into equal-width intervals.
SecondsFrequency
\(10\le t\lt 15\)6
\(15\le t\lt 20\)5
\(20\le t\lt 25\)2
\(25\le t\lt 30\)6

  1. How many readings are below 20 seconds?

    [2]

  2. Describe a frequency diagram that represents these data.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Add the first two group frequencies. The boundary value itself belongs in the next interval.

\(11\)

(b) The intervals have the same width. The vertical axis can show frequency for each whole interval.

Draw adjacent bars of width 5 seconds, with heights 6, 5, 2, 6.

examples.title: Read values from a stem-and-leaf diagram
examples.question:
These are game scores. The key is \(7\mid 3\) means 73.
StemLeaves
61 3
73 6
84 6

  1. Find the median score.

    [2]

  2. Find the range.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) There are six scores. Use the third and fourth values, 73 and 76. Add and halve.

\(\frac{149}{2}\)

(b) Use the key to read the greatest and least scores. Subtract the least from the greatest.

\(25\)

examples.title: Read change across weeks
examples.question:
A centre records its visitors at the same time each week.
WeekVisitors
120
223
324
427

  1. How much higher is the last total than the first total?

    [2]

  2. Name a suitable display for these readings. Name a different display for paired temperature and visitor counts taken on the same days.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Compare the final week with the first week. The difference is the last value minus the first.

\(7\)

(b) A time series keeps the time order. A scatter graph shows each pair together to reveal a possible relationship.

A time series graph for weekly totals, and a scatter graph for paired temperature and visitor count.

examples.title: Check a pictogram’s scale
examples.question:
A designer uses a fixed key. Each complete badge represents 10 items.
BadgeNumber of badges
Reusable bottles5
Refill packs1

  1. How many items are shown by the Reusable bottles badges?

    [2]

  2. The designer proposes a different-sized badge for Refill packs but no new key. What should you check?

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Each of the 5 badges represents 10. Multiply.

\(50\)

(b) A larger drawing can exaggerate its value. Keep an unambiguous unit.

The picture needs a clear, consistent scale so its size does not imply extra or fewer items.

lessons.title: Comparing data and checking predictions
lessons.summary: Compare centres and spread and explain what a sample can tell you.
lessons.objective: Compare centres and spread and explain what a sample can tell you.
lessons.before: A value with frequency five contributes five copies to the total.
lessons.ideas:
Multiply each value by its frequency. Add the products and divide by the total frequency. For median, use positions in the ordered list. For mode, find a value with highest frequency.

Use a measure of centre, such as median or mean, together with the range. The range is the greatest value minus the least value.

Compare fair measures, such as proportions for different sample sizes. Discuss one plausible source of variation. Recommend a useful change to the method if questions remain.
lessons.method:
Show the sum of the frequencies you used.

Name both groups and use measurements from both to support each comparison.

Use cautious language about a sample and avoid claiming a cause from a pattern alone.
mistakes: Dividing by the number of distinct values ignores repetition.
An identical median does not guarantee every value is close to that median.
A pattern in a small sample may not hold for the whole population.

examples.title: Find the mean using counts
examples.question:
A group records the frequency of each score.
ScoreFrequency
122
151
182

  1. Work out the mean score.

    [2]

  2. Find the median and explain why.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Multiply each score by its frequency to find the total. There are 5 scores.

Equal counts are 3 below and 3 above 15, so those changes cancel.

\(15\)

(b) The counts on either side match, with at least one score at the centre.

\(15\)

examples.title: Compare the centre and spread of two groups
examples.question:
Two groups measure the same quantity.
GroupOrdered readings
A\(25,\;27,\;27,\;27,\;29\)
B\(24,\;27,\;27,\;27,\;30\)

  1. Give the difference between the two ranges.

    [2]

  2. Use a measure of centre and a measure of spread to compare the groups.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The A range is 4. The B range is 6. Subtract the ranges.

\(2\)

(b) A centre alone cannot show how spread out the values are.

Both medians are 27 and both modes are 27. Group B has the greater range.

examples.title: Test a prediction and discuss variation
examples.question:
Two groups each test 49 seeds. Group A counts 9 sprouted seeds. Group B counts 10. The project asks whether two soil types support different sprouting rates.

  1. What is the difference between the two proportions that sprouted?

    [2]

  2. Explain one reason to collect more data before drawing a firm conclusion.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Both groups have the same number tested, so subtract the two counts and divide by the number tested in one group.

\(\frac{1}{49}\)

(b) A difference for these samples alone does not tell us which factor caused it.

Other factors, such as light, water or differences between seeds, can cause variation. Repeat the test with larger, comparable samples.

questions.prompt_html:
Two groups each test 47 seeds. Group A counts 12 sprouted seeds. Group B counts 17. The project asks whether two soil types support different sprouting rates.

  1. What is the difference between the two proportions that sprouted?

    [2]

  2. Explain one reason to collect more data before drawing a firm conclusion.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(\frac{5}{47}\)

(b) Other factors, such as light, water or differences between seeds, can cause variation. Repeat the test with larger, comparable samples.
questions.solution_html:
(a) Both groups have the same number tested, so subtract the two counts and divide by the number tested in one group.

\(\frac{5}{47}\)

(b) A difference for these samples alone does not tell us which factor caused it.

Other factors, such as light, water or differences between seeds, can cause variation. Repeat the test with larger, comparable samples.
